claims.text: Enhanced lattice distortion is a primary governor of hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys.
Local chemical short-range ordering is a primary governor of hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Local chemical short-range ordering impedes dislocation motion.
Deliberately modifying composition can increase atomic size mismatch.
Deliberately modifying composition can promote local chemical short-range order.
Moderate temperatures can provide a regime in which recovery does not override the proposed strengthening effects.
XRD peak broadening and atomic displacement parameters can quantify the extent of lattice distortion.
Atom probe tomography can quantify the degree of chemical short-range ordering.
Increased atomic size mismatch introduces larger lattice distortions.
The evolution of local chemical short-range order provides additional dislocation-pinning sites.
Lattice distortion and short-range-order pinning jointly hinder dislocation motion.
Hindered dislocation motion increases alloy hardness.
Hindered dislocation motion increases alloy yield strength.
Modified alloys with greater atomic size mismatch and promoted short-range order will have higher hardness than the baseline alloy.
Modified alloys with greater atomic size mismatch and promoted short-range order will have higher yield strength than the baseline alloy.
Hardness and yield strength are predicted to increase by approximately 10–30% relative to the baseline.
Hardness and yield strength will correlate positively with measured lattice distortion.
Hardness and yield strength will correlate positively with measured chemical short-range order.
In multiphase alloys or at elevated temperatures where recovery dominates, strengthening mechanisms other than lattice distortion and short-range order may become significant.
